title: How Do Hummingbirds Survive the Night? 🐦
description:
How do hummingbirds survive the night without food? Their hearts can hit 1,200 beats a minute, so at night they drop into torpor, cooling their bodies and slowing their heartbeat to around 50 beats a minute until sunrise.

topic: The Hummingbird Paradox: how does a bird that tiny not starve overnight?
script: Hummingbirds almost shut down every night, and you never notice. Why would a heart drop from twelve hundred beats to fifty? Their tiny engine burns fuel so fast they can sip three times their weight in nectar a day. But at night, there's no nectar. A long night without food could starve them. So they drop into torpor. Their body cools from a hundred and five degrees by almost fifty. Their heartbeat crashes to around fifty a minute. Some even hang upside down, stiff as a statue. One Andes species chills to just thirty-eight degrees Fahrenheit, barely above freezing. It slows their metabolism by up to ninety-five percent. At sunrise, they shiver their flight muscles and warm up for about an hour. Then it's off to breakfast. So would you rather shut down every night like a hummingbird, or eat three times your weight every day?
key_facts: Hummingbird heart rate: typically 500 to 1,200 bpm awake (Birds & Blooms); torpor can drop it below 50 (Journey North) or as low as 40 (Smithsonian)
Normal body temperature about 105°F; in torpor it can drop almost 50 degrees (Journey North)
Black metaltail in the Andes let its body temperature fall to 38°F (Smithsonian, Biology Letters study)
Costa's hummingbird can slow its metabolism by up to 95% in torpor (Birds & Blooms)
Ruby-throats can eat up to three times their weight in nectar a day (Birds & Blooms)
Rewarming takes about an hour (Journey North); they shiver/vibrate flight muscles to warm up
